name: Make rope from natural fibres
blurb: Reverse-wrap two bundles of plant fibre and you get cordage strong enough to matter. It is the technique behind every rope made before industry.
gear: Fibrous plants: nettle, dogbane, yucca, lime bast, or even long dry grass
A knife, and water for retting
steps: Harvest and process the fibre: for nettle or dogbane, dry the stalks, then split and scrape away the woody pith to leave long fibres.
Buff the fibres by rolling them between your hands to soften and separate them.
Take a bundle, twist it until it kinks in the middle, and fold it there — this is your start.
Reverse-wrap: twist the upper strand away from you, then cross it over the other towards you, and repeat. The counter-twist is what locks the rope together.
Splice in new fibre before a strand runs out, staggering the joins so they never coincide.
Test it to destruction to learn how much your cordage actually holds.
tips: Consistent twist tension is what makes a rope strong. Loose sections are where it breaks.
Staggering the splices matters more than anything else for strength.
Learn to identify your fibre plants confidently — nettles are excellent, and some lookalikes are not.
proof: A metre of two-ply cordage that holds your own body weight in a static pull.
